marks: According to Islamic tradition Muhammad received his first revelation in the cave of Hira near Mecca (around 610); the Kaaba is the focus of prayer and pilgrimage.
The Hijra: Muhammad and his followers moved here in 622, the start of the Islamic calendar; he died in Medina in 632.
Founded around 670; its Great Mosque is among the oldest in North Africa.
Husayn, Muhammad's grandson, was killed here in 680, an event central to Shia Islam.
The Dome of the Rock was completed here in 691–692.
Founded in 762 as the capital of the Abbasid caliphs, a great centre of learning.
The Great Mosque of Córdoba, begun in 785, in the capital of the Umayyads of al-Andalus.
Al-Azhar, founded in 970–972 under the Fatimids, one of the oldest seats of learning in the world.
The gravestone of Sultan Malik al-Salih (1297) is the earliest evidence of a Muslim ruler in Southeast Asia.
Mansa Musa of Mali made his famous pilgrimage in 1324; Timbuktu's Djinguereber mosque was built on his return.
The Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, and Hagia Sophia became a mosque.
Granada, the last Muslim kingdom of Spain, surrendered in 1492.
The Moriscos, descendants of the Muslims of Spain, were expelled between 1609 and 1614.
The Taj Mahal, built (1632–1648) by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife.
Usman dan Fodio's jihad (1804) founded the Sokoto Caliphate.
notes: According to Islamic tradition Muhammad receives his first revelation near Mecca (610) and moves to Medina (622); by his death in 632 most of Arabia accepts his rule, and the caliphs' armies conquer Syria, Iraq, Egypt and Persia.
The Umayyad caliphate reaches from Spain to Sindh and Central Asia; the Abbasids found Baghdad (762). Conversion is gradual: for centuries many subjects remain Christian, Jewish or Zoroastrian.
Baghdad is a centre of learning; al-Bukhari gathers the hadith; by most estimates Muslims become the majority in Iran and Iraq in the 9th and 10th centuries.
The Fatimids found Cairo and al-Azhar (970); the Volga Bulgars (922) and the Kara-Khanid Turks of Central Asia accept Islam.
The Seljuk Turks defeat Byzantium at Manzikert (1071) and settle Anatolia; in West Africa the rulers of Takrur, Gao and Kanem become Muslims.
Sufi orders spread; Saladin retakes Jerusalem (1187); Muslim merchants settle the Swahili coast and the ports of India and China.
The Delhi Sultanate is founded (1206); the Mongols sack Baghdad (1258), and within decades the Mongol rulers of Iran and the Golden Horde become Muslims.
Mansa Musa of Mali makes his pilgrimage (1324); Islam spreads in northern Sumatra and Malacca; Ibn Battuta travels from Morocco to China.
The Ottomans take Constantinople (1453); Granada, the last Muslim kingdom of Spain, falls (1492); Islam spreads through the Malay world and Java.
Three great empires: the Ottomans, the Safavids, who make Iran Shia (from 1501), and the Mughals in India (from 1526).
Spain expels the Moriscos (1609–1614); the Taj Mahal is built (1632–1648); Makassar and other kingdoms of eastern Indonesia accept Islam.
Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab allies with the House of Saud (1744); Russia annexes the Crimea (1783).
Usman dan Fodio founds the Sokoto Caliphate (1804); by the end of the century European powers rule most Muslim lands.
Turkey abolishes the caliphate (1924); most Muslim countries gain independence; millions of Muslims settle in Europe and North America.
About 2 billion Muslims (2020), the second-largest religion; the largest Muslim country is Indonesia.
